strengths: The paper addresses a practical failure of seam cutting: changing the seam cannot reliably fix poorly aligned structures. Repairing selected patches with dense correspondences and reconnecting local seams through fixed boundary labels is a useful, modular approach.

Experiments cover 79 image pairs across three datasets. Figures 1, 10, and 11 show visible improvements in curb, pavement, and stair continuity. The proposed method also receives 108 of 160 first-place votes in the selected user-study examples.
The runtime comparisons use common hardware and indicate substantial savings over iterative seam estimation [17] on difficult examples, supporting the practical motivation for selective local repair.

The pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript credits its principal components and external datasets. Section 4.4 and Figure 12 provide a useful, candid account of failures involving large residual displacement.
weaknesses: The technical advance over existing seam-guided alignment remains insufficiently established. The method combines the seam-quality evaluation of [17], SIFT flow, sigmoid weighting, and constrained graph cuts. There are no systematic ablations establishing the benefits of selective component extraction or the proposed flow modification over simpler local refinement. Figure 4 provides only a single-example comparison of sigmoid settings.

Quantitative comparisons are restricted to two seam-cutting methods [16,17], whereas the proposed method additionally changes image alignment. Comparisons with seam-driven approaches [18,26] are limited to qualitative examples, and other relevant alignment approaches cited in the manuscript are not evaluated. Consequently, the experiments establish improvement over fixed-alignment seam cutting more convincingly than advancement over competing parallax-handling pipelines. Compatibility with arbitrary alignment and seam-cutting methods is also untested beyond the chosen initialization.

Independent evidence of perceptual improvement is limited. Equation (5) closely matches the SSIM criterion used to select repairs and does not measure geometric distortion or object preservation; the manuscript itself reports disagreement between this metric and visual quality. The user study helps, but its eight manually selected 'controversial' examples introduce selection concerns. Selection rules, presentation randomization, and uncertainty across images are not reported.

The claim that the method can 'almost remove' the rough-alignment assumption exceeds its demonstrated scope. Section 3.4 assumes small local residual parallax, and the repair strategy requires an initially mostly satisfactory seam. Moreover, the acceptance condition max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) classifies a uniformly high-error seam as plausible. The acknowledged limitations appropriately describe local residual repair, but they substantially qualify the broader contribution claim.

The central warp is underspecified for reproduction. Section 3.4 writes f(V) while Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid of normalized horizontal position, without explicitly defining the resulting vector field. Handling other seam orientations and overlapping patch updates is also unclear. The assertion that false-positive repairs cannot worsen results lacks a stated rejection mechanism or systematic experimental support.

There are secondary reporting errors: Figures 6, 8, and 9 label baselines as [21] and [19], inconsistent with the methods discussed in the text. Table 1 gives 159 and 161 total rankings for [17] and [16], respectively, although each should receive 160 under the described protocol. These are correctable issues, distinct from the substantive validation concerns.
